questions.stem: Which change meets the biological definition of evolution?

options.text: The frequency of a heritable characteristic changes in a population over several generations
options.why: Evolution is change in a population's heritable characteristics across generations.

options.text: An athlete develops larger muscles after following a demanding training program
options.why: That's an acquired change within one lifetime. It doesn't change the population's inherited characteristics.

options.text: A plant grows taller after receiving more light and mineral nutrients
options.why: That's an environmental effect on one plant's phenotype. A population hasn't undergone a heritable change.

options.text: A bird learns a new feeding behavior by watching other members of its group
options.why: That's learned behavior within an organism's lifetime. It isn't evidence that inherited characteristics have changed.

questions.stem: Two species have very similar DNA base sequences in the same genes. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: They share a relatively recent common ancestor
options.why: Inherited sequences accumulate differences after lineages split, so greater similarity generally supports more recent common ancestry.

options.text: They must occupy the same ecological niche
options.why: Related species can occupy very different niches. Sequence similarity concerns ancestry, not current resource use.

options.text: They are members of one interbreeding population
options.why: Different species can have similar sequences while remaining reproductively isolated. Similarity doesn't demonstrate interbreeding.

options.text: They independently evolved identical sequences under similar selection pressures
options.why: Independent evolution can produce analogous traits, but extensive sequence similarity is stronger evidence of inheritance from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: Why does selective breeding provide evidence for evolution?

options.text: Repeated selection changes the heritable characteristics of a population across generations
options.why: Selected parents pass alleles for desired characteristics to offspring, changing the population over generations.

options.text: Domesticated organisms acquire useful characteristics because humans provide better conditions
options.why: Better conditions can alter an individual's phenotype, but selective breeding depends on inherited variation and differential reproduction.

options.text: Humans create every desired allele when they choose which individuals will reproduce
options.why: Selection acts mainly on heritable variation already present. Choosing parents doesn't create each desired allele.

options.text: All members of a domesticated species develop the selected characteristic during their lives
options.why: That's an acquired-change explanation. Selective breeding changes the proportion of inherited characteristics across generations.

questions.stem: Which observation identifies two structures as homologous?

options.text: They share an underlying structural plan inherited from a common ancestor
options.why: Homology is based on common evolutionary origin, even when the structures now perform different functions.

options.text: They perform the same function with different underlying anatomical structures
options.why: That describes analogous structures produced by convergent evolution, not homologous structures.

options.text: They occur in organisms exposed to similar environments and selection pressures
options.why: Similar pressures can produce convergence in unrelated lineages. Environment alone doesn't establish shared origin.

options.text: They have identical external shapes despite belonging to distantly related organisms
options.why: External resemblance can evolve independently. Homology depends on ancestry and underlying structure.

questions.stem: Bird wings and insect wings are analogous as structures for flight. Why?

options.text: They perform the same function but evolved from different ancestral structures
options.why: Similar selection pressures favored flight structures independently, which is convergent evolution.

options.text: They have the same arrangement of bones inherited from one winged ancestor
options.why: Insect wings don't contain the tetrapod limb bones found in bird wings. They didn't inherit one wing structure from a recent common ancestor.

options.text: They perform different functions despite sharing the same evolutionary origin
options.why: That describes divergence of homologous structures. Both examples here perform flight but have different origins.

options.text: They became structurally identical after the two populations exchanged alleles
options.why: Birds and insects don't exchange alleles. Their flight structures evolved independently.

questions.stem: Which event distinguishes speciation from evolutionary change within a single species?

options.text: Populations become reproductively isolated
options.why: Reproductive isolation prevents gene flow and marks the formation of separate species.

options.text: A heritable characteristic becomes more common
options.why: That can occur while every member remains part of one interbreeding species.

options.text: Natural selection favors one phenotype
options.why: Natural selection can change a single population without splitting it into separate species.

options.text: Several individuals migrate to another habitat
options.why: Migration alone isn't speciation. Gene flow may continue unless a reproductive barrier develops.

questions.stem: What was the first direct effect of the Congo River on the ancestral populations of bonobos and common chimpanzees?

options.text: It reduced interbreeding and gene flow between the populations
options.why: The river acted as a geographical barrier. Once gene flow was restricted, the populations could diverge under different selection pressures.

options.text: It created new alleles for survival on each side of the river
options.why: A river doesn't direct mutations to make useful alleles. Mutation produces variation without regard to what organisms need.

options.text: It made every individual develop a different set of acquired characteristics
options.why: Acquired characteristics aren't the mechanism. Isolation changed gene flow between populations.

options.text: It caused immediate sterility in hybrids produced by the two populations
options.why: Geographical isolation came first. Reproductive incompatibilities developed through later divergence.

questions.stem: Which example could initiate sympatric speciation?

options.text: Two groups in the same area begin breeding in different seasons
options.why: Different breeding times create temporal isolation even though the groups occupy the same geographical area.

options.text: A mountain range divides a population into eastern and western groups
options.why: A physical barrier creates geographical isolation, so this could initiate allopatric speciation.

options.text: Individuals move freely between two habitats and mate randomly throughout the population
options.why: Free interbreeding maintains gene flow, which works against divergence into separate species.

options.text: Two separated populations experience identical conditions and exchange migrants each generation
options.why: Ongoing migration mixes alleles, and identical conditions don't provide the differential selection described here.

questions.stem: How does adaptive radiation increase biodiversity?

options.text: One ancestral species diversifies into several species adapted to different niches
options.why: Vacant niches create different selection pressures, allowing related species to specialize and coexist with less competition.

options.text: Several unrelated species independently evolve the same feature in one niche
options.why: That's convergent evolution. Adaptive radiation produces several divergent species from one ancestral species.

options.text: One species becomes better adapted while continuing to occupy its original niche
options.why: That may be evolution within one species, but it doesn't describe radiation into multiple species.

options.text: Hybridization combines all local species into one population with a shared gene pool
options.why: Combining gene pools would reduce distinct species. Adaptive radiation involves divergence and reproductive isolation.

questions.stem: Courtship signals prevent individuals of two animal species from mating. What type of barrier is this?

options.text: A prezygotic behavioral barrier
options.why: The behavioral difference prevents mating before fertilization, so no hybrid zygote forms.

options.text: A postzygotic sterility barrier
options.why: Postzygotic sterility affects a hybrid after fertilization. Here, mating never occurs.

options.text: A geographical barrier
options.why: The animals can encounter one another. Their courtship behavior, rather than physical separation, blocks mating.

options.text: A temporal barrier
options.why: Temporal isolation involves reproduction at different times. This example concerns courtship signals.

questions.stem: Why is a mule normally unable to transfer alleles between horse and donkey populations?

options.text: Its chromosomes cannot pair and separate normally during meiosis, so it is sterile
options.why: Horse and donkey chromosome sets aren't fully homologous in a mule, which disrupts meiosis and functional gamete production.

options.text: Its chromosomes replicate by mitosis before any gametes can be produced
options.why: Chromosome replication and mitosis occur in fertile organisms too. The problem is unsuccessful homologous pairing during meiosis.

options.text: Its parents contribute identical chromosome sets that prevent genetic variation
options.why: The parental chromosome sets differ rather than being identical. Their incompatibility disrupts meiotic pairing.

options.text: Its courtship behavior prevents the horse and donkey from mating in the first place
options.why: A mule already resulted from mating and fertilization. Its sterility is a postzygotic barrier.

questions.stem: How can chromosome doubling restore fertility in an interspecific plant hybrid?

options.text: It gives each chromosome a homologous partner for pairing during meiosis
options.why: Balanced pairing can allow the allopolyploid to produce functional gametes and reproduce with other compatible polyploids.

options.text: It removes every chromosome inherited from one of the two parent species
options.why: That would remove a parental chromosome set rather than duplicate it. Allopolyploidy retains sets from both species.

options.text: It converts all chromosome differences into acquired characteristics of the hybrid
options.why: Chromosome doubling is a heritable genomic change. It doesn't turn genetic differences into acquired traits.

options.text: It allows unrestricted mating with both original diploid parent species
options.why: The new chromosome number usually creates reproductive isolation from the diploid parents, which is why speciation can occur.
